title: 7. A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

q.t: The three angles of any triangle add up to…
q.e: Angle sum property: a line through the top vertex parallel to the base shows the three angles fill a straight angle.

q.t: Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 70°. The third is…
A triangle with all three sides equal is called…
q.e: Equi-lateral = equal sides.

q.t: A triangle with exactly two equal sides is called…
q.e: Isosceles triangles have two equal sides.

q.t: Can 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm make a triangle?
q.e: The two shorter sides together (7) can't reach across 8, so the arcs never meet.

q.t: Can 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm make a triangle?
q.e: The longest side 5 is less than 3 + 4 = 7, so the triangle inequality holds.

q.t: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is…
q.e: All three angles are equal and add to 180°, so each is 60°.

q.t: A triangle with one angle of exactly 90° is called…
q.e: One right angle makes a right-angled triangle.

q.t: What tool lets you mark all points 4 cm from a point A?
q.e: A compass draws a circle/arc — every point on it is the same distance (the radius) from the centre.

q.t: ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60° in ∆ABC. Find the exterior angle at C.
q.e: Exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles: 50 + 60 = 110°.

q.t: Can 10, 15, 30 be the sides of a triangle?
q.e: Going directly from one end of the 30 side to the other would be longer than the roundabout path of 25 — impossible.

q.t: Can 3, 6, 9 be the sides of a triangle?
o: No — 3 + 6 equals 9, so the points lie on a line
q.e: When the two shorter sides exactly equal the longest, the arcs only touch on the base: a flat line, not a triangle.

q.t: Two angles of a triangle are 90° and 30°. The third is…
Can 35° and 150° be two angles of a triangle?
o: No — they already add to more than 180°
q.e: Two angles of a triangle must add to less than 180°; here 185°.

q.t: In ∆ABC, ∠A = 50° and ∠B = ∠C. Find ∠B.
q.e: ∠B + ∠C = 130°, shared equally → 65° each.

q.t: Which test is enough to check three lengths make a triangle?
o: Longest side < sum of the other two
Shortest side < sum of the other two
Longest side > sum of the other two
q.e: If the longest side passes, the shorter ones automatically do, since each is already less than the longest.

q.t: What is an altitude of a triangle?
o: The perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side
A line from a vertex to the middle of the opposite side
q.e: An altitude measures the height: it meets the opposite side (extended if needed) at 90°.

q.t: In the angle-sum proof, why is ∠XAB equal to ∠B?
o: They are alternate angles, since XY ∥ BC
q.e: AB is a transversal of the parallel lines XY and BC; alternate angles are equal.

q.t: Can a triangle have angles 70°, 70°, 70°?
q.e: The angles of every triangle add to exactly 180°.

q.t: Two angles are 75° and 45°. The third angle is…
Two sides of a triangle are 3 cm and 7 cm. The third side must be…
q.e: It must be less than the sum (10) and more than the difference (4), or the longest side would fail the test.

q.t: ∠A = 40°. What is the smallest ∠B for which ∠A and ∠B can NOT be angles of a triangle (with AB as the included side)?
q.e: At 140° the ray from B is parallel to the ray from A (same-side interior angles add to 180°), so they never meet.

q.t: Can 1, 100, 100 be the sides of a triangle?
q.e: Check the longest side: 100 < 101. A very thin isosceles triangle.

q.t: An exterior angle of a triangle is 120° and one opposite interior angle is 45°. The other opposite interior angle is…
q.e: Exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles: 120 − 45 = 75°.

q.t: Why does an acute-angled triangle need ALL three angles acute?
o: Every triangle already has at least two acute angles
So that it can be equilateral
q.e: Two angles of 90° or more would already reach 180°, so every triangle has at least two acute angles — 'one acute angle' tells nothing.

q.t: Which isosceles triangle is obtuse-angled?
q.e: 120° is obtuse, and two angles (30°) are equal so two sides are equal.

q.t: Can an equilateral triangle be right-angled?
o: Only if its sides are 5 cm
q.e: Its three equal angles share 180°, so each is 60°.

q.t: Which set can be the sides of a triangle?
q.e: Longest side 25 < 10 + 20 = 30. The others fail: 35 > 30, 8 > 6, 5 > 4.

q.t: The circles from A and B (radii = the two shorter sides, AB = the longest) just touch at one point. Then…
o: sum of shorter sides = longest side, no triangle
q.e: Touching means the radii add up exactly to AB: the 'third vertex' lies on AB, so the shape is flat.

q.t: Two angles of a triangle are 150° and 15°. The third is…
q.e: 180 − 165 = 15°: an obtuse isosceles triangle.

q.t: In a triangle, the angles are x, 2x and 3x. Find x.
In ∆ABC, ∠B = 90° and ∠A = 35°. Find ∠C.
q.e: ∠A + ∠C = 90° in a right triangle, so ∠C = 55°.

q.t: An exterior angle is 130° and the two opposite interior angles are equal. Each is…
q.e: The two opposite interior angles add to the exterior angle: 130 ÷ 2 = 65°.

q.t: Why does the exterior angle equal the sum of the two opposite interior angles?
o: Both make 180° with the same interior angle
q.e: ∠A + ∠B + ∠ACB = 180 and ∠ACD + ∠ACB = 180, so ∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B.

q.t: Which two angles CAN be angles of a triangle?
q.e: Only 90 + 85 = 175 is less than 180. The others reach 180° or more.

q.t: Sides 5 and 5: which can NOT be the third side?
q.e: The third side must be less than 5 + 5 = 10. At exactly 10 the triangle is flat.

q.t: How many different right triangles have ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm?
q.e: ∠A can be any angle between 0° and 90° (with ∠C = 90° − ∠A), each giving a different triangle.

q.t: In an obtuse-angled triangle, where can the altitude from a vertex at the acute end fall?
o: Outside the triangle, on the extended opposite side
q.e: When the angle at the foot is obtuse, the perpendicular lands beyond the side, so we extend the side first.

q.t: A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles. So the four angles of the quadrilateral add up to…
q.e: A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles, each 180°: total 360°.

q.t: Lengths 4, 5, 8: the circles of radius 4 (from A) and 5 (from B) with AB = 8 …
o: cross at two points — a triangle exists
q.e: 4 + 5 = 9 > 8, so the circles overlap: a point 4 cm from A on AB is only 4 cm from B, inside the 5 cm circle.
